questions.question: When will quantum computers actually be useful?

hybrid.answer:
He says quantum is already starting to give value in small, limited ways, with the first real quantum advantage expected around 2026 and transformational, fault-tolerant machines by 2030. This is the roadmap he describes for IBM, and his latest talk here is from October 2025.

**Most recent (Oct 2025):** Describing IBM's roadmap, he says that by next year (2026) there will be the first provable quantum advantage on some application, and by 2030 the first fault-tolerant quantum computer [1]. He frames the 2030 machine as one that implements universal quantum computing and brings the transformational impact, which he puts at about five years away, "this decade" [2]. He also notes he doesn't yet have proof that the HSBC result he cites couldn't be done classically [3].

**Earlier (May 2025):** He gave the same two-step timeline: first quantum advantage in 2026, meaning real advantage on real systems that classical computing alone can't deliver, and real transformational power by 2030 [4]. He says the first applications are likely in chemistry and catalysis, such as simulating complex enzymes [5].

**Useful today, in a limited way:** In March 2025 he said that with today's non-error-corrected machines, errors can be mitigated, so scaling is still exponential but slower, and that "you can get already value today". He says current use is simulating small molecules [6]. He also points to progress in error rates, from about 1 in 10 years ago to nearly 1 in 10,000 [7].

**Why he trusts the timeline:** He says the test of whether a technology is real is whether it has a roadmap it keeps hitting, and he says IBM has "never missed a point" on its roadmap since 2016 [4][8].

**Not covered:** The videos available here don't confirm whether the 2026 advantage has actually been demonstrated, since the latest one is from October 2025.
